roles.title: Senior Full Stack Developer
roles.description:

What you'll do: design and build full-stack web apps and SaaS platforms with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Node.js / NestJS; model data in PostgreSQL; integrate payments, auth, third-party APIs and AI features; set up CI/CD, testing and cloud hosting on AWS or Vercel; review code, mentor developers and turn client requirements into clear technical plans.

What we look for: 5+ years building and shipping production web applications; deep JavaScript/TypeScript, React and Node.js; solid SQL, REST/GraphQL API design and Git; experience with cloud deployment and performance tuning; clear written English for working with international clients. articles.title: Why we still argue about page speed
articles.alt: Website on laptop, tablet and phone
articles.author: ASPR Global Tech Team

blocks.text: A beautiful website that takes six seconds to load on a phone is losing you customers every day. Here's why speed is a business decision, not a technical detail — and how to fix it.

Most visitors arrive on a phone, on mobile data — test for them, not for office Wi-Fi.
Google uses Core Web Vitals in rankings, so slow pages also get found less.
Set a performance budget before design starts, not after launch.
Images, fonts and third-party scripts cause most slowdowns — and are the easiest to fix.
Why speed matters more than you think

Your customers rarely see your site the way it looked in the design review. They open it on a mid-range phone, on a patchy connection, often while doing something else. What they see is a blank screen, then a layout that jumps, then a button that moves just as they tap it. Many simply leave.
Speed affects three things at once: how many visitors stay, how many of them enquire or buy, and how high you rank on Google. A slow site quietly costs you leads you never knew you had.
The three numbers Google checks

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — how quickly the main content appears. Aim for under 2.5 seconds.
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — how fast the page reacts when someone taps or clicks. Aim for under 200 ms.
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — how much the page jumps while loading. Aim for under 0.1.
If the page is beautiful but nobody waits for it, it isn't beautiful. It's empty.
What we do on every build

We agree a performance budget at the very start: how heavy each page can be, how many scripts it can carry and how fast it must load on a real Android phone. Design decisions are made inside that budget — not argued about after launch.

Serve images in modern formats (WebP/AVIF) at the size the screen needs
Limit fonts to two families and preload them
Remove or delay third-party scripts that don't earn their place
Render pages on the server so content shows before JavaScript loads
Test on a cheap phone over 4G, not just a laptop
Re-check Core Web Vitals in Google Search Console after launch
Quick test: open your site on your phone with Wi-Fi off. If you'd lose patience, so do your customers. Free tools like Google PageSpeed Insights show exactly what's slowing it down.
The bottom line
Speed isn't a nice-to-have for developers — it's a sales number. A fast site keeps more visitors, converts more of them and ranks higher. Build it in from day one and it costs almost nothing extra.

articles.title: A logo test that takes ten seconds
articles.author: ASPR Global Tech Team

blocks.text: Before a logo goes anywhere near a client presentation, it has to pass a ten-second test. Most first drafts fail — and that's exactly why we run it.

A logo spends most of its life small: app icons, profile pictures, favicons.
If it doesn't work in one colour, it doesn't really work.
A memorable mark is one people can sketch after seeing it once.
Testing early is far cheaper than reprinting signage later.
Where your logo actually lives

We tend to judge logos large, centred on a white slide. Real life is harsher: a 16-pixel browser tab, a WhatsApp display picture, a stamp on a carton, a sign seen from across the road. A mark that only works big mostly doesn't work at all.
The ten-second test

Shrink it — view it at favicon size (16–32 px). Is it still recognisable?
Strip the colour — print it in solid black. Does the shape still hold?
Look away — glance for one second, then sketch it from memory. Could you?
A good mark is the one your customer can draw from memory after seeing it once.
What the test usually catches

Thin lines that disappear at small sizes
Gradients that turn muddy in print or on fabric
Lettering so detailed it becomes a smudge
Shapes that look like a competitor's when simplified
Before you approve a logo

Seen it as a favicon and an app icon
Seen it in one colour, on light and dark backgrounds
Seen it on a mock-up of your real sign, packaging or uniform
Asked someone outside the project to sketch it from memory
Received vector files (SVG, EPS, PDF) and simple usage rules
Small businesses can't buy recognition with big ad budgets — the logo has to do the work on its own. Ten seconds of honest testing is the cheapest brand insurance there is.
The bottom line
Judge your logo where it will really live, not on a perfect slide. If it survives small, single-colour and from-memory, it's ready for the world.

SEO can bring the right people to your website. It can't make them trust you, stay, or pick up the phone. Knowing the difference saves months of disappointment — especially now that AI answers sit above search results.

Rankings only help if the page already convinces visitors to act.
In 2026, Google and AI assistants favour clear, specific, trustworthy pages.
Fix the website first, then technical SEO, then content.
SEO is a 3–6 month investment that compounds — not a switch.
Problems SEO can't solve

A homepage that doesn't explain what you do in five seconds
Prices or next steps hidden behind long forms
No reviews, case studies or proof you're real
A phone number or WhatsApp button that's hard to find on mobile
A slow, outdated site that looks untrustworthy
If these are present, more traffic simply means more people leaving. That's why our SEO work always starts with the website itself.
How search changed

Google and AI assistants now summarise answers directly on the results page. To be the source they quote, your pages need real, specific information — your services, your locations, your prices or price ranges, and direct answers to real customer questions. Thin pages written only for keywords get skipped.
SEO brings people to the door. Your website still has to open it.
What SEO genuinely does well

Complete and verify your Google Business Profile
Fix speed, mobile issues and broken pages
Add structured data (schema) so Google understands your business
Write one helpful page per service and per location you serve
Answer your customers' real questions in plain language
Track enquiries, not just traffic
Ask any SEO provider one question: "How will this bring more enquiries, not just more visitors?" A good answer starts with your website, not with keywords.
The bottom line
Treat SEO as the amplifier, not the fix. Make the site worth visiting first — then good SEO brings steady enquiries without paying for every click.

articles.title: The scope document that saved a project
articles.author: ASPR Global Tech Team

blocks.text: Halfway through a build, a client asked for "just one more feature". A two-page scope document we had both signed turned a potential argument into a ten-minute conversation.

Scope creep arrives as small, reasonable-sounding requests.
A good scope lists what's included — and what isn't.
New ideas become phase-two items, not silent delays.
A clear scope protects the client most of all.
How scope creep really happens

It rarely starts with a big request. It's another user role, a second language, an export to Excel. Each one is small. Together they can double the timeline, blow the budget and sour a good relationship.
What goes in our scope document

The goal of the project, in the client's own words
Exactly what we will build — pages, screens, features
What we will not build in this phase
Integrations and third-party services involved
Price, payment milestones and timeline
How change requests are handled and priced
A written "not in this phase" at the start is kinder than a surprise invoice at the end.
What happened next

When the new request arrived, we opened the document together. The feature wasn't in it. We priced it as a phase-two item, the client agreed, and the original launch date held. Nobody had to remember who said what on a call months earlier.

Is the goal written in plain language?
Is there an explicit "not included" list?
Are milestones tied to payments?
Is there a simple process for change requests?
Have both sides signed it before design starts?
Hiring any agency or freelancer? Ask to see the scope before you pay a deposit. If there isn't one, that's your first warning sign.
The bottom line
A scope document isn't paperwork — it's how you stay in control. You know exactly what you're paying for and can make trade-offs with full information, instead of discovering them at launch.

articles.title: Choosing boring technology on purpose
articles.alt: App icons on a dark home screen
articles.author: ASPR Global Tech Team

blocks.text: Every month brings a new framework, database or AI tool promising to change everything. For client work we deliberately choose proven technology — and use new tools only where they clearly help.

Your product should still be maintainable five years from now.
Proven tools mean easier hiring, better security and lower long-term cost.
New technology must earn its place on our own projects first.
AI is used where it solves a real problem, not as decoration.
Why "boring" is a feature

A business website or app should outlive the team that built it. That means choosing tools with large communities, long support windows and plenty of developers who already know them — so you're never locked to one agency.
Our default stack

Web: Next.js, React and TypeScript
Back end: Node.js / NestJS or Python / Django
Data: PostgreSQL
Mobile: Flutter or React Native
Hosting: AWS or Vercel
Games: Unity
Clients pay for software that works on a Tuesday afternoon — not for our curiosity.
Where we do use new tools

Standing still isn't the goal. AI coding assistants speed up our development, automated tests catch problems early, and AI features — chatbots, document search, smart forms — go into products where they genuinely help users. When a newer tool has a clear advantage for a specific project, we explain the trade-off in plain language and write it into the scope.

Is the technology widely used and actively maintained?
Can other developers maintain it if we're not around?
Does it have a clear security and update track record?
Is the code and hosting in your name?
Is there a real reason to choose something newer?
Before you sign with any developer, ask: "If you disappeared tomorrow, how easily could someone else take over?" The answer tells you a lot about their technology choices.
The bottom line
Boring by default, never boring by accident. Proven foundations keep your product stable and affordable; new tools are added only where they make a measurable difference.

articles.title: Hiring for skill, not certificates
articles.alt: Developer writing code on a laptop
articles.author: ASPR Global Tech Team

blocks.text: ASPR started because a talented learner didn't fit a classroom. That story still shapes how we hire: show us what you've built, and we'll care far less about where you studied.

Real work predicts job performance better than certificates.
Our process: portfolio, a short task, a team conversation, a written offer.
Self-taught and career-switching candidates are welcome.
Clients benefit because their team was hired for what it can actually do.
Why we look at work first

Some of the best developers and designers we know are self-taught. They learned by building for friends, local shops and their own curiosity. A traditional CV filter would have rejected most of them in seconds.
How our hiring works

Send work, not a template CV — a live site, app, design file, repository or reel
A short task that looks like real client work
A conversation with the people you'd actually work with
An offer in writing, with clear role, pay and start date
Your portfolio is your degree here.
Tips if you're applying

Lead with your best two or three pieces, not everything
Explain what you did, the problem, and the result
Include links that work — GitHub, live sites, Behance, YouTube
Show something you learned on your own
Keep your message short and specific to the role
No portfolio yet? Build one small, real thing for a local business or a friend. One finished project beats ten unfinished tutorials.
The bottom line
Hiring for skill takes more time per candidate, but it builds a team that can deliver. And a studio that keeps learning keeps its clients' products current.

faqs.question: How do we start a project with you?
faqs.answer: Send a brief through the form, WhatsApp or call. We reply within one working day and set up a Discover call — scope, price and timeline follow in writing. The call is free, takes about 30 minutes, and is scheduled in your time zone. You don't need a finished spec — an idea and a goal are enough to start.

faqs.question: Who will we actually be talking to?
faqs.answer: One point of contact across all ten services — the specialists doing the work, with no middle layer. You get a shared channel (WhatsApp, Slack or email — your choice) and a weekly update. When a question is technical, the developer or designer on your project answers it directly.

faqs.question: Do you work with clients in the US and other countries?
faqs.answer: Yes. We work with clients in the US, UK, Europe, the Middle East and India. Calls are scheduled in your time zone, and you wake up to progress on the staging link. Quotes are in US dollars, and contracts, invoices and payments are handled online — no travel needed.

faqs.question: Can you work alongside our existing team?
faqs.answer: Yes. We can take one workstream — say the app, the brand or SEO — and work to your team's tools, repos and review process, with a shared channel and a weekly check-in. We follow your coding standards and branching rules, and everything we build is documented so your team can take it over at any time.

faqs.question: How do you price a project?
faqs.answer: After the Discover call we write down the scope, price and timeline, and you sign them off before any build starts. Quotes are in US dollars, or your local currency on request. Most projects are a fixed price paid in milestones, so you always know what the next payment is for. If the scope changes later, we price the change separately — no surprise bills.

faqs.question: What does a typical website cost?
faqs.answer: It depends on pages, features and integrations. A focused business website usually starts under $5,000; sites with e-commerce, booking or custom dashboards typically fall in the $5,000–$15,000 range. You get a fixed written quote after the Discover call. Every site includes mobile-friendly design, basic SEO setup and a handover walkthrough at no extra cost.

faqs.question: How long does a build take?
faqs.answer: A business website typically takes 3–6 weeks, a mobile app or SaaS MVP 8–16 weeks, and a brand identity 2–4 weeks. The signed timeline in your scope document is the one we work to. You get a staging link from week one, so you can watch progress instead of waiting for a big reveal.

faqs.question: Do you take projects in phases?
faqs.answer: Yes. Larger replacements are quoted in phases, and app builds can price phase one on its own. Phase one usually delivers a working core you can launch or show investors. You decide on each next phase with real usage and feedback in hand.

faqs.question: What exactly do we get on handover?
faqs.answer: The source code in a repository you own, design files, admin logins, domain and hosting access, a short how-to guide or video walkthrough, and a list of every third-party service and what it costs. We also run a live handover session with your team, so nobody is left guessing how anything works.

faqs.question: Do we own the code and accounts?
faqs.answer: Yes. You own everything — code, designs, domains and accounts. Accounts are opened in your name from day one, not moved over at the end. If you ever change partners, you can take it all with you — no lock-in and no hidden licence fees.

faqs.question: What happens if something breaks after launch?
faqs.answer: Every launch has a rollback ready, and we stay on the account after the invoice clears. Urgent issues get a response within one working day, and bugs in our own work are fixed free. We also set up uptime monitoring, so we often know about a problem before you do.

faqs.question: Do you offer ongoing support plans?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every launch includes a period of fixes at no charge. After that, an optional monthly care plan covers updates, security patches, backups, uptime monitoring and a set amount of small changes. You can pause or cancel the plan any month — no long contracts.

faqs.question: Can you handle app and web together?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ten services sit under one roof, so app, web, brand and SEO come from one team on one timeline. Shared design and shared code keep the app and the website looking and working the same. You also get one invoice and one point of contact instead of three agencies.

faqs.question: Which technologies do you build on?
faqs.answer: React, Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind on the front end; Node.js, NestJS, Python and Django on the back end; Flutter, React Native, Kotlin and Swift for mobile; Unity for games; PostgreSQL, MongoDB and SQLite for data; AWS and Vercel for hosting. We pick proven, widely used tools, so any good developer can maintain your product later. Where it helps, we add AI features such as chatbots, smart search and automation.

faqs.question: Do you do brand work without a build?
faqs.answer: Yes. Logo, graphics and video are services on their own. You get print-ready and web-ready files plus simple brand guidelines, so anyone can use your brand correctly. Many clients start with a brand and come back for the website once it's ready.

faqs.question: Can you fix a project someone else started?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. We start with a paid code and infrastructure audit, tell you plainly what can be kept, what should be rebuilt, and what it will cost, and only then quote the work. The audit report is yours to keep, even if you decide not to continue with us. We've taken over half-finished sites, apps and stores — and we don't judge the last team's work in front of you.
